opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think the key thing is that once a robot is actually out there doing a job, it's going to encounter situations that nobody anticipated when we collected its training data. You can bootstrap a lot from demonstrations, from imitation learning, from pretraining on large amounts of web and video data, and that gets you a robot that's competent. But competent isn't the same as good, and it's certainly not the same as reliable at the level you'd need for real deployment.

Imitation learning has this fundamental ceiling: the robot can only be as good as the data it was shown, and in practice it's often a bit worse, because small errors compound. It drifts into states the demonstrator never visited, and then it doesn't know what to do. Reinforcement learning is different in kind. It lets the robot learn from its own experience, from the consequences of its own actions. So when it makes a mistake on the job, that mistake becomes data. It can figure out that a particular grasp tends to slip, or that a certain way of approaching an object works better, and it can get better than the person who taught it.

There's also a practical argument. When a robot is deployed, it's generating an enormous amount of experience every day. If you're only doing imitation, all that experience is mostly wasted unless a human comes in and labels or corrects it. With RL, even a fairly coarse signal, like whether the task succeeded or a person stepping in to intervene, can be turned into improvement. That's how people learn on the job, too. Somebody shows you the basics, but you really get good by doing it, messing up, and adjusting.

And I'd add that I don't see this as RL versus everything else. The way I think about it, the pretrained model and the demonstrations give you the prior, the common sense, the starting point that makes RL tractable in the real world. Ten years ago, RL from scratch on a physical robot was painfully slow. Now, starting from a strong foundation model, the robot only has to do a relatively small amount of refinement, and that makes learning on the job actually feasible. That combination is, I think, where things really get exciting.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think the fundamental reason is that reinforcement learning is really the only framework we have that's actually about learning from your own experience. Everything else, supervised learning, imitation learning, you're learning from somebody else's data. And that works great when you have a lot of it and when the distribution of situations the robot is going to encounter matches what was in the dataset. But robots in the real world are going to run into things nobody anticipated. The lighting is different, the object is slightly deformed, the gripper is a little worn. And when that happens, a policy that was trained purely by imitation has no mechanism to get better. It just fails, and it keeps failing the same way.

Whereas with RL, the robot has a signal that tells it whether what it did actually worked. So every time it's out there doing the job, it's also collecting data about its own mistakes, and it can close that loop. I think of it a bit like the difference between a student who has read a textbook and a student who has actually practiced. The textbook gets you a long way, but the practice is what gets you to the level where you're actually reliable.

And there's a scaling argument too. If you're deploying thousands of robots, the amount of experience they're generating dwarfs anything you could collect through teleoperation. If you can't learn from that experience, you're leaving the most valuable data source on the table. The imitation data gets you off the ground, but RL is what lets the robot keep improving after you've shipped it.

Now, the honest caveat is that doing this in the real world is hard. You have to handle the fact that exploration can be unsafe, that rewards are hard to specify, that the data is off-policy and messy. A lot of my group's work has been about making RL robust enough to actually work in that regime, things like offline RL, where you learn from whatever data you have without needing to actively explore in a dangerous way. But I think the direction is pretty clear. If you want robots that get better the longer they're deployed, there's really no substitute for learning from their own experience, and that's what RL is.

astra-6.text:
The big advantage is that a robot can learn from the consequences of its own actions. If you train it only to imitate people, then whenever it encounters a situation it doesn’t know how to handle, you need somebody to show it what to do. That’s a pretty serious bottleneck if you want robots to keep improving after they’re deployed.

With reinforcement learning, you can instead tell the robot what constitutes success. Suppose it’s trying to pick something up. It can try, observe whether it actually picked the object up, and use that experience to improve. A failed attempt becomes useful training data, even though nobody demonstrated the correct action in that particular situation.

Of course, you don’t want a robot learning entirely from scratch in someone’s home. You would want it to start with a very capable policy, probably trained using demonstrations and other data. Reinforcement learning then gives it a way to improve that policy through experience. The difficult part is making that improvement safe and making sure the signal you give it actually captures what you want.

sol-6.1.text:
Because when a robot is learning on the job, what it naturally gets is experience: it takes an action, something happens, and it can observe the result. It doesn’t necessarily have somebody standing next to it telling it what the correct action should have been at every moment.

Reinforcement learning gives you a way to learn from that experience. If the robot tries to pick something up and fails, that failure can become useful training data, provided it can tell whether it succeeded. With imitation learning, you typically need a person to supply another demonstration.

Of course, that puts a lot of pressure on how you set up the learning process. You need a useful signal of success, and exploration has to be safe. I wouldn’t want a robot to learn everything from scratch in somebody’s home. You’d start with a capable policy, perhaps trained from demonstrations, and then use reinforcement learning to improve it as it encounters the particular situations that arise on the job.
